summary: Describes conventions for using several cryptographic algorithms with the CMS encrypted key package content type, covering the EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, and AuthEnvelopedData structures.

plainLanguage.summary: The locked box for keys can use different kinds of locks. This says which locks to use and how.

questions: algorithms for cms encrypted key package
what algorithms does cms encrypted key package use
aes key wrap with padding requirement
subtitle: Which encryption, key management and signature algorithms to support when protecting cryptographic keys in CMS.

tldr.problem: The CMS encrypted key package content type needs agreed algorithm choices so implementations can interoperate when carrying cryptographic keys.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets MUST and SHOULD algorithms for EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, AuthEnvelopedData and SignedData, led by AES Key Wrap with Padding. It defines no new algorithms.
tldr.outcome: Conforming implementations share a baseline of AES-128 key wrap, RSA and SHA-256, with 1024 to 2048 bit public keys. The unit metadata says RFC 6161 updates this document.

today: RFC 6033 is a Proposed Standard that is updated by RFC 6161, and no RFC is listed as obsoleting it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6033 gives conventions for using cryptographic algorithms with the CMS encrypted key package content type from RFC 6032. It covers EnvelopedData and EncryptedData (RFC 5652) and AuthEnvelopedData (RFC 5083), and later adds SignedData and key sizes.

It does not define any new algorithms. It points to algorithms defined elsewhere and says which are required (MUST), recommended (SHOULD) or optional (MAY).
sections.plainLanguage: It is a shopping list of locks, with must-have, should-have and nice-to-have items.

sections.title: EnvelopedData and EncryptedData
sections.content:
For EnvelopedData, implementations MUST support key transport, with RSA encryption required and RSAES-OAEP recommended. They SHOULD support key agreement, with Ephemeral-Static Diffie-Hellman required if key agreement is used.

Whatever key management is chosen, AES-128 Key Wrap with Padding MUST be supported as the content-encryption algorithm, and AES-256 Key Wrap with Padding SHOULD be. With key agreement, the key wrap algorithm for the content-encryption key must match the AES size of the content-encryption algorithm. EncryptedData leaves key management to other means, so only the content-encryption algorithm applies, with the same MUST and SHOULD.
sections.plainLanguage: Keys are wrapped in a special key-only lock. Which lock size you use for the key box decides the lock size for the inner key.

sections.title: AuthEnvelopedData and SignedData
sections.content:
AuthEnvelopedData has the same key management requirements as EnvelopedData; the difference is the content-encryption algorithm. Implementations MUST support 128-bit AES-GCM and SHOULD support 256-bit AES-GCM. They MAY also support AES-CCM.

For SignedData, implementations MUST support RSA signatures and SHOULD support RSASSA-PSS and DSA. They MUST support SHA-256 together with these schemes and SHOULD support SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: Some boxes also carry a tamper seal, and signed notes need a stamp. The list says which seals and stamps must work.

sections.title: Key Sizes and Security
sections.content:
If an implementation supports RSA, RSAES-OAEP, DH, RSASSA-PSS or DSA, it MUST support key lengths from 1024 bits to 2048 bits, inclusive.

The security considerations of the referenced algorithm documents apply. The key wrap choice follows RFC 5649, which favours a mechanism used only to protect keying material. The RFC says no AES-GCM or AES-CCM mode provides that property, and that it will be updated if one is defined.
sections.plainLanguage: Locks must come in sizes from medium to big. Key-only locks are preferred because they keep keys apart from other data.
